message.content:
## What this is and why it matters for «говорить»

«Говорить» is an imperfective verb, so its present tense actually covers two jobs at once: describing what happens *now* (I speak) and what happens *habitually/generally* (I speak Russian). Since it's imperfective, it has no simple future — the future must be built with «быть» + infinitive. This pattern is extremely common, so mastering it here pays off for hundreds of other imperfective verbs.

## The pattern

«Говорить» is a Class II (second-conjugation) verb. Take the stem **говор-** and add the second-conjugation endings: **-ю́, -и́шь, -и́т, -и́м, -и́те, -я́т**. Note the spelling rule: after a consonant, the 1st person plural/3rd plural ending is written with **-я** instead of **-а** because the stress falls on it (this is just how -ать/-ить verbs with stressed endings behave in this class — compare «люби́ть» → «лю́бят» with unstressed ending vs. «говоря́т» with stressed ending).

Stress in the present tense sits **on the ending in every form**, never retreating to the stem — this is a fixed, end-stressed pattern typical of many -ить verbs of this type.

Since «говорить» is imperfective, the future is **periphrastic**: conjugate «быть» in the future (бу́ду, бу́дешь, бу́дет, бу́дем, бу́дете, бу́дут) and add the imperfective infinitive «говори́ть» unchanged. The stress on «бу́ду/бу́дешь/etc.» falls on the stem of «быть», while «говори́ть» keeps its own infinitive stress on the final syllable.

## The forms

| | Present | Future |
|---|---|---|
| я | говорю́ *(I speak/am speaking)* | бу́ду говори́ть *(I will speak/be speaking)* |
| ты | говори́шь *(you speak)* | бу́дешь говори́ть *(you will speak)* |
| он / она́ / оно́ | говори́т *(he/she/it speaks)* | бу́дет говори́ть *(he/she/it will speak)* |
| мы | говори́м *(we speak)* | бу́дем говори́ть *(we will speak)* |
| вы | говори́те *(you [pl./formal] speak)* | бу́дете говори́ть *(you will speak)* |
| они́ | говоря́т *(they speak)* | бу́дут говори́ть *(they will speak)* |

## In the wild

- «Он говори́л ти́хо, но я всё слы́шал.» → "He spoke quietly, but I heard everything." — past tense here for context, but note the same stem; present would be «Он говори́т ти́хо» (he speaks quietly — a habitual trait).
- «Не говори́ никому́.» → "Don't tell anyone." — this is actually the imperative («не говори́»), included here only to flag it's *not* present tense despite looking similar; present tense «ты говори́шь» would mean "you speak/are speaking."
- «Ты говори́шь по-ру́сски?» → "Do you speak Russian?" — present tense, ты-form, classic A1 question.
- «Я бу́ду говори́ть с ним за́втра.» → "I will speak with him tomorrow." — future tense, periphrastic construction with «бу́ду» + infinitive.

## Watch out

- Don't confuse the imperative «говори́!/говори́те!» (Speak!) with the 2nd person present «говори́шь/говори́те» — they look alike but the imperative drops the personal ending pattern differently in stress/context.
- Learners often forget the future needs **two words**: «бу́ду говори́ть», not a single conjugated form — «говори́ть» itself never changes in the future, only «быть» does.
- Watch the -я́т (not -а́т) ending in «они́ говоря́т» — a common spelling slip.
- Memory hook: "Bu-du + infinitive" — think of «бу́ду» as a helper who always brings the infinitive along unchanged, like a passport that never expires.

## Check yourself

1. How do you say "We will speak" in Russian?
2. Why is «говоря́т» spelled with я instead of а?
3. What's wrong with saying *«Я говорю́ бу́ду с тобо́й»* for "I will speak with you"?

---
1. «Мы бу́дем говори́ть».
2. Because the ending is stressed, and stressed endings after a consonant in this class use я, not а.
3. Word order/construction is wrong — it should be «Я бу́ду говори́ть с тобо́й»; «бу́ду» must come before the infinitive «говори́ть».
